title: Two Kinds of Pain
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: Macbeth (Shakespeare): ambition, power and tragedy
source: Written for english/y9 lesson 39 ('Two Kinds of Pain' (teacher-written article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 39: Non-fiction: guilt and shame. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: Two Kinds of Pain
paras: Psychologists often separate two painful feelings. Guilt says, 'I did something bad.' Shame says, 'I am bad.' The difference matters. Guilt points to an action, so it can be repaired: we apologise, make amends and change. Shame points to the whole self, so it tends to make people hide, deny or lash out.
This is why guilt, though uncomfortable, can be healthy. It is conscience doing its job. The danger comes when guilt is ignored for too long: it does not disappear, it goes underground.

Imagine two pupils who have both been unkind to a classmate. The first feels guilty: she cannot stop thinking about the hurt look on her classmate's face, so the next day she apologises. The second feels ashamed: he decides he is simply a bad person, so there is no point saying sorry, and he avoids the classmate altogether. The same mistake leads to opposite endings.

Buried guilt can show itself in strange ways: in sleeplessness, in sudden anger, in a mind that keeps returning to the same scene. Writers have known this for centuries. Literature is full of characters who cannot wash away what they have done.

The healthiest response is not to feel nothing, but to listen to guilt early, while it is still pointing at something we can fix. Many faiths teach the same: sincere regret, making amends and resolving not to repeat a wrong open the door to forgiveness.
Guilt is a warning light. Shame is a fog. One shows us the way back; the other hides it.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Guilt is healthy because it points to an action we can repair; shame is harmful.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: Contrast in short quoted sentences ('I did something bad' / 'I am bad'); the two-pupil example; the metaphors 'goes underground', 'warning light' and 'fog'.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: With a balanced pair of metaphors that sum up the difference.

questions.q: Define guilt and shame in your own words, using the article.
questions.a: Guilt: feeling bad about something you did, which you can repair. Shame: feeling bad about who you are, which makes you hide.
Ignored guilt is hidden but still there and will come back.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain how the writer makes the difference clear. Use two methods, then apply it to Lady Macbeth. Starter: 'The writer uses contrast to...'
questions.a: Two methods (contrast of short quotations, metaphor 'goes underground') and an application to Lady Macbeth.

questions.q: Extend: is Macbeth driven more by guilt or shame by Act 3? Explain.
questions.a: Shame: he hides and lashes out, killing more to feel safe.

questions.q: Stretch: why is repentance absent from the play?
questions.a: Macbeth chooses to go further in blood instead of turning back, which makes his story a tragedy.

questions.q: According to the article, why can guilt be healthy?
options: It points to an action that can be repaired
questions.a: C) It points to an action that can be repaired. Guilt is about actions and leads to repair; hiding belongs to shame.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: A good sign if it leads to repentance and repair; dangerous if ignored.
